scene: Difficult intubation with apneic oxygenation. SpO2 still 99%.
question: What is rising?
why: Oxygen keeps flowing in, but nothing clears CO2. PaCO2 jumps in the first minute of apnea, then keeps climbing about 3 mmHg a minute, so pH falls while SpO2 looks perfect.
pearl: Oxygenation is not ventilation. A great SpO2 can hide a rising CO2.
caption:
Six minutes of apnea and the SpO2 is still 99%. So what's quietly climbing? 🫁

Comment your pick before the answer 👇

Apneic oxygenation keeps oxygen moving in, but nothing washes CO2 out. PaCO2 rises fast in the first minute, then roughly 3 mmHg every minute after, and the pH drifts down even while the oximeter looks perfect.

slides.title: The RV can't take a sudden pressure load.
slides.sub: Acute RV failure and massive PE: recognize it, protect perfusion.

slides.body: A sudden rise in PVR dilates the RV, pushes the septum left and underfills the LV. Output falls, and so does RV coronary perfusion.

bullets: Dilated RV, flattened septum on echo
Keep systemic BP up: vasopressor early
slides.pearl: A dilated RV rarely needs more volume. It needs pressure and lower PVR.

slides.body: Call for help early. Options include thrombolysis, catheter-directed therapy, surgical embolectomy or ECMO, per your PE team and institution.

slides.title: Pressure, not volume.
slides.body: Support the RV before it spirals.

caption:
Sudden hypotension, SpO2 falling, ETCO2 dropping off a cliff. Is the right ventricle giving out? 🫀

Swipe for the essentials: why a thin-walled RV fails under a sudden pressure load → how massive PE shows up in the OR → how to protect the RV with early vasopressor support, not big fluid boluses → when to call for definitive clot treatment.

💡 A dilated RV pushes the septum into the LV. More volume can make output worse.

scene: Sevo case. ETCO2 climbing despite double the ventilation.
question: Most likely cause?
why: FiCO2 of 0 rules out the absorbent, and more ventilation should have brought ETCO2 down. Rising ETCO2 plus tachycardia under a volatile is MH until proven otherwise: stop triggers, call for help, give dantrolene.
pearl: Check FiCO2 first. If it's zero, the CO2 is coming from the patient.
caption:
You doubled the minute ventilation and the ETCO2 is still climbing. Inspired CO2 is zero. What now? 🔥

Comment your pick before the answer 👇

A zero FiCO2 rules out exhausted absorbent, and more ventilation should have lowered the number. Rising ETCO2 with tachycardia under a volatile is malignant hyperthermia until proven otherwise: stop triggers, call for help, 100% O2 at high flow, and get dantrolene.

scene: Tourniquet just released after a 2-hour knee case.
question: Most likely cause?
why: Release sends cold, acidotic, CO2-rich blood back from the limb and drops SVR. Expect a transient fall in BP with a rise in ETCO2 and potassium. Have volume and a vasopressor ready.
pearl: Warn the team before the tourniquet goes down, not after.
caption:
Tourniquet down after two hours, and the BP drops to 74/40 while the ETCO2 creeps up. What just happened? 🦵

Comment your pick before the answer 👇

Tourniquet release washes cold, acidotic, CO2-rich blood back into the circulation and drops SVR. Expect a transient fall in BP, a rise in ETCO2 and potassium, and sometimes emboli. Have volume and a vasopressor ready, and bump the ventilation.

slides.title: Can't intubate. Can't oxygenate. Now what?
slides.sub: When to move to front-of-neck access.

slides.body: Intubation, supraglottic airway and face mask have failed, and SpO2 is falling. Naming it moves the whole team.

bullets: Call for help and the airway cart
Extend the neck, find the membrane
Slide a bougie along the blade
Railroad a 6.0 cuffed tube, confirm ETCO2
slides.pearl: Can't feel the membrane? Vertical skin incision first, then find it by touch.
Repeated attempts burn time and swell the airway.

slides.title: Know the neck before you need it.
slides.body: Find the cricothyroid membrane on every airway exam.

caption:
Failed tube, failed supraglottic, failed mask, and the SpO2 is falling. When do you pick up the scalpel? 🔪

Swipe for the essentials: declare CICO out loud → full neuromuscular block and 100% O2 from above → scalpel-bougie-tube through the cricothyroid membrane → why waiting for one more attempt costs the most.

💡 Can't feel the membrane? A vertical skin incision first, then find it by touch.

scene: Preeclampsia, laboring. Platelets 104k this morning, now 82k.
question: Epidural now?
answer: B. Yes, with a recent count
why: SOAP consensus supports neuraxial at 70k or more if there's no other coagulopathy or antithrombotic. With a falling trend, use a fresh count and place it early, before the window closes.
pearl: The trend matters as much as the number. An early epidural can avoid a crash GA.
caption:
Preeclampsia, platelets 104k this morning and 82k now. Do you place the epidural? 🤰

Comment your pick before the answer 👇

The SOAP consensus supports neuraxial at 70,000 or more when there's no other coagulopathy and no antithrombotic on board. With a falling count, get a recent value and place it early: a working epidural can spare her a general anesthetic and a difficult airway later.
